interactions.label: In the retinoid embryopathy case, craniofacial, cardiac, and thymic defects all

params.question: In the retinoid embryopathy case, craniofacial, cardiac, and thymic defects all resulted from a single drug taken in the first trimester. What best explains why multiple organ systems were affected?

answers.text: Retinoids selectively accumulate in craniofacial, cardiac, and thymic tissues

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Retinoid embryopathy is not caused by selective tissue accumulation. The drug was present systemically; the key factor is when each organ was forming, not where the drug concentrated.

answers.text: The drug crossed the placenta at different times during the first trimester

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The drug was continuously present after ingestion. The variable is not when the drug arrives but which organs are in their critical period of formation at that time.

answers.text: Each affected organ was in its critical period of active formation during the exposure window

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Each organ system has its own critical period — the developmental window when it is actively forming and most susceptible to disruption.

answers.text: The mother's immune response to the drug targeted these specific organ primordia

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Teratogenesis from retinoids is a direct effect on embryonic development, not an immune-mediated process. The explanation lies in the timing of organ formation, not maternal immunity.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key concept is critical periods. Each organ system is most vulnerable when it is actively being formed. A teratogen present across multiple such windows can independently affect several organs.
Exactly. The concept of critical periods explains why a single teratogen can damage multiple organs — each system has its own vulnerable window during active formation.

interactions.label: During which period of prenatal development are structural malformations most li

params.question: During which period of prenatal development are structural malformations most likely to result from teratogenic exposure?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Organogenesis occurs during weeks 3–8, when all major organ systems are being laid down for the first time. This makes it the window of greatest susceptibility to structural defects.
During weeks 1–2, the response is typically all-or-none: the embryo either recovers fully or fails to implant. Structural malformations are not characteristic of this early window.

By week 9, major organ systems are already established. Teratogenic exposure during the foetal period more commonly causes growth restriction or functional deficits rather than structural malformations.
The neonatal period begins after delivery. Prenatal teratogenic effects on organ formation cannot occur once the baby has been born.

overallFeedback.feedback: The embryonic period (weeks 3–8) is the window of organogenesis — all major organ systems are being established for the first time, making it the period of greatest susceptibility to structural malformations.
Correct. All major organ systems are first laid down during weeks 3–8, making the embryonic period the most vulnerable window for structural birth defects.

params.question: The accepted biological lower limit of foetal viability is 22–24 weeks, yet in much of India the practical threshold is closer to 26–28 weeks. What primarily explains this gap?

answers.text: Indian law prohibits neonatal resuscitation before 28 weeks of gestation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: No such law exists. The MTP Act governs termination of pregnancy, not neonatal resuscitation. There is no legal barrier to treating premature neonates at any gestational age.

answers.text: Foetal lung maturation follows a slower timeline in tropical populations

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Lung maturation follows the same developmental timeline regardless of geography or climate. The gap is due to healthcare infrastructure, not biological variation.

answers.text: The World Health Organization defines viability as beginning at 28 weeks

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The WHO actually uses a 22-week threshold. India registers births and stillbirths from 28 weeks onward, but that is a registration threshold, not a viability definition.

answers.text: Many Indian hospitals lack the advanced neonatal intensive care required to support survival at 22–24 weeks

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Survival at 22–24 weeks demands specialised neonatal intensive care — ventilatory support, surfactant therapy, continuous monitoring — that is unavailable in many Indian hospitals.

overallFeedback.feedback: The gap exists because survival at 22–24 weeks requires sophisticated neonatal intensive care that many Indian hospitals do not have, pushing practical viability to 26–28 weeks.
Exactly. Viability is not purely a biological threshold — it depends on the healthcare infrastructure available to support extremely premature neonates.

params.question: Alcohol, unlike most other teratogens, has no known safe threshold of exposure during pregnancy.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is true. While most teratogens follow a dose-response curve with a definable threshold, alcohol is a notable exception. No safe level of alcohol consumption during pregnancy has been identified, making complete abstinence the only reliable preventive measure.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. Wilson's principles note that most teratogens show a dose-response relationship with a threshold below which no effect is seen. Alcohol is a critical exception — no safe level of consumption during pregnancy has been established, which is why complete abstinence is recommended.
